title: Adjectives with irregular comparison
lede: *good*, *better*, *best* — and the adjectives whose comparative splits into two words with different jobs.
intro: Almost every gradable adjective compares with *-er/-est* (*taller*) or *more/most* (*more careful*). A handful do neither, and their forms have to be learned: *good*, *better*, *best*; *bad*, *worse*, *worst*. Several also split into two words with different jobs — *farther* for distance and *further* for degree, *older* for age and *elder* for family rank, *later* for time and *latter* for the second of two — so each form has its own entry.

title: The -ing and -ed pairs
lede: *boring* and *bored*, *interesting* and *interested* — what causes a feeling, and who has it.
intro: The *-ing* adjective describes what causes a feeling; the *-ed* adjective describes the person who has it. *The movie was boring*, and so *I was bored*. Russian often uses one word for both, and *I am boring* — which says something unkind about the speaker — is one of the most common mistakes in learner English. Both members of each pair are here, next to each other, with examples that make the difference impossible to miss.

title: Adjectives that only follow a verb
lede: *afraid*, *asleep*, *alive*, *alone* — adjectives that can come after *be* but never before a noun.
intro: These adjectives can follow a verb — *the baby is asleep* — but cannot stand before a noun: never *an asleep baby*. Most of them begin with *a-* because they grew out of old prepositional phrases (*asleep* was once *on sleep*), and each entry gives the word that does the job before a noun instead: *a sleeping baby*, *a living animal*, *a frightened child*.

title: Adjectives that only go before a noun
lede: *main*, *mere*, *former*, *utter* — adjectives that stand before a noun and cannot follow a verb.
intro: The mirror image of the previous group: these go before a noun and cannot follow a verb. *The main reason* is English; *the reason is main* is not. Several of them are emphasizers that add force rather than a quality (*a mere child*, *sheer luck*, *an utter disaster*), and a few change meaning when they do appear after a verb, which each entry points out.

title: Extreme and absolute adjectives
lede: *freezing*, *huge*, *delicious*, *unique*, *dead* — adjectives that already mean *very*, or that are simply true or not.
intro: Extreme adjectives already contain *very* — *freezing* means *very cold* — so they take *absolutely*, *completely* or *really*, never *very*: *absolutely freezing*, not *very freezing*. Absolute adjectives name a state that is either true or not (*dead*, *unique*, *pregnant*) and resist comparison, although real American usage bends that rule, and the entries say where.

title: Adjectives that change meaning after the noun
lede: *the members present*, *the people involved*, *the city proper* — adjectives that can follow a noun, and what that does to them.
intro: A small set of adjectives can follow the noun they describe, and several of them mean something different there. *The present members* are the current ones; *the members present* are the ones in the room. *A concerned parent* is worried; *the parents concerned* are the ones involved. Each entry gives both positions and both meanings, side by side.

title: Adjectives that take a fixed preposition
lede: *proud of*, *good at*, *interested in*, *similar to* — the adjectives that bring their own preposition.
intro: The preposition after these adjectives is not chosen for its meaning — it is simply the one the adjective takes: *afraid of*, *good at*, *interested in*, *married to*. Russian uses different prepositions or a case ending, so the English one has to be learned with the word. Every entry names its preposition, says when a different one changes the meaning (*angry at* a person, *angry about* a thing), and links to the full pattern in the preposition dictionary.

title: Adjectives with a to-infinitive or that-clause
lede: *easy to use*, *likely to rain*, *glad that you came*, *kind of you to help*.
intro: These adjectives take a *to*-infinitive or a *that*-clause: *easy to use*, *likely to rain*, *glad that you came*. Two traps run through the group. *It is kind of you* judges a person but *it is important for you* states a need, and a few adjectives — *essential*, *vital*, *imperative* — take the bare verb in their *that*-clause: *it is essential that he be there*.

title: Spelling changes in comparison
intro: The comparative and superlative are regular, but the spelling is not. One-syllable adjectives ending in consonant–vowel–consonant double the last letter (*big*, *bigger*); a final *-y* becomes *-i-* (*happy*, *happier*); a final *-e* just takes *-r* (*nice*, *nicer*); and a few two-syllable words take *-er* where learners expect *more* (*simpler*, *narrower*, *quieter*). Each entry spells both forms out.

title: Nationalities and other proper adjectives
intro: In English, adjectives of nationality, religion and origin are always capitalized — *Russian*, *American*, *Catholic* — where Russian writes them in lowercase. Many of them also work as nouns for a person (*a Russian*) or a language (*Russian*), and a few have a separate noun altogether (*Polish*, but *a Pole*; *Dutch*, but *a Dutchman*). These entries cover the adjective and flag the nouns that differ.

title: Colors, shapes and materials
lede: *gray*, *navy*, *oval*, *wooden* — the adjectives that sit last before the noun.
intro: Colors, shapes and materials sit near the end of the adjective order, just before the noun: *a big round wooden table*. Colors compare, and some shapes only loosely (*rounder* is fine; *more square* is common). For materials, English often uses the noun itself (*a cotton shirt*, *a glass door*) rather than an adjective; the entries here are the true adjectives, such as *wooden* and *woolen*, and they note where the noun is the normal choice.

title: Compound adjectives
lede: *well-known*, *part-time*, *old-fashioned*, *a five-year plan* — two words working as one.
intro: Compound adjectives join two or more words into a single modifier, and the hyphen is part of the grammar: *a well-known author*, but *the author is well known*. Number compounds take a singular noun — *a five-year plan*, never *a five-years plan* — which is the error a Russian speaker is most likely to make with this group.

title: Adjectives that end in -ly
intro: These words end in *-ly* but are adjectives, not adverbs: *a friendly dog*, *a lonely night*. Most of them have no adverb form at all, so *she smiled friendly* is wrong and English needs a phrase instead: *she smiled in a friendly way*. A few — *daily*, *weekly*, *early* — are both, and those entries show each use.

title: False friends for Russian speakers
lede: *actual*, *sympathetic*, *accurate*, *intelligent* — English adjectives that look Russian and mean something else.
intro: These look like Russian words and mean something else. *Actual* is not *актуальный* — it means *real* — and *sympathetic* is not *симпатичный*, it means *understanding*. *Accurate* means *precise*, not *аккуратный*; *intelligent* means *clever*, not *интеллигентный*. Each entry puts the trap first and gives the English word that does mean what the Russian one does.

title: Adjectives that are easily confused
intro: Pairs built on the same root that mean different things: *economic* is about the economy, *economical* is about saving money; *historic* means *important in history*, *historical* means *about the past*. Native speakers mix some of these up too, but in writing they matter, and each entry names its partner and the test that separates them.

title: Adjectives used as nouns with the
lede: *the rich*, *the young*, *the homeless* — adjectives that name a whole group of people.
intro: With *the*, some adjectives stand for a whole group of people: *the rich*, *the young*, *the homeless*. The group is always plural — *the rich are*, never *the rich is* — and it cannot take a plural *-s* (*the riches* is a different word). For one person, English needs a noun: *a homeless man*, not *a homeless*.
